name: Sortition
summary: Sortition is the selection of decision-makers by random draw from the citizen body instead of by election. Its advocates hold that lots give every citizen an equal chance of holding political power, produce bodies that mirror the public, and escape campaign money, party machines and elite capture. Proposals range from replacing every elected legislator (lottocracy), through a lot-chosen chamber beside an elected one, to lot-chosen juries that only oversee officials.

scope: The modern movement for choosing political decision-makers by lot, as the scholarship names it: lottocracy (Guerrero, as set out in Jakobi's dissertation), bicameral legislature by lot (Gastil and Wright), sortition as anti-corruption oversight (Bagg), and the citizens' assemblies whose members are drawn by lot (Gasiorowska). Ancient Athenian practice is a historical precedent covered by Athenian democracy, and the wider deliberative-democracy tradition is a separate subject; neither answers here. Sortition is a method for selecting rulers, so the defining sources take positions mainly on democratic institutions, and most statements stay null.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Gastil and Wright propose a legislative assembly of randomly selected citizens, and Jakobi and Gasiorowska treat lot-chosen citizens' assemblies deliberating on public questions as sortition's working form.

corporate-influence.rationale: Gastil and Wright cite lobbyist influence and wealth-funded campaigns as electoral failings, and Bagg says wealthy elites and powerful private actors can ensure officials are sympathetic to their interests.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Jakobi defines democracy as self-government that elections alone do not constitute and that can exist without them, and Gastil and Wright argue elected legislatures fall short of the democratic ideal.

natural-rulers.rationale: Jakobi presents lottocracy as regarding everyone as capable and worthy of holding political office, and Gastil and Wright put the burden of proof on anyone who would exclude citizens as unfit.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Lottocrats such as Guerrero and Landemore replace all elected legislators with lot-chosen ones, but Gastil and Wright say sortition need not replace elections and keep an elected chamber, and Bagg limits lots to oversight tasks.

one-party-rule.rationale: Under sortition every voter-eligible person is eligible for office and access to it is distributed equally by lot, which a party holding exclusive leadership of the state contradicts.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Gastil and Wright present sortition as drawing ordinary citizens directly into legislating, though only those selected take part, and say direct participation has a place in an ideal democratic system.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Gastil and Wright say elections attract candidates with an excess of ambition and ego, and Jakobi reports lottocrats' view that elected politicians respond more to special influences than to their electorate.

property-franchise.rationale: Gastil and Wright's inclusion principle asks a democracy to include all persons in the political unit, and they pair their design with universal automatic voter registration.

racial-franchise.rationale: Gastil and Wright's inclusion principle asks a democracy to include all persons in the political unit, and they pair their design with universal automatic voter registration.

second-chamber.rationale: Gastil and Wright make a lot-chosen chamber the complement of an elected one, while Jakobi describes the lottocratic alternative that abolishes the elected parliament, so the proposals under the name split.

notes: Built from five saved sources: Gastil and Wright's essay, Jakobi's dissertation on Guerrero's lottocracy, Bagg's AJPS article, Gasiorowska's study of citizens' assemblies, and Wikipedia as a finding aid. Sortition is a method of selecting officeholders, so its sources answer only on selection, representation, equality of access, parties, elite capture and the franchise; every economic, cultural, ecological, technological and foreign-policy statement is null. Themes searched: elections and parties, expertise versus ordinary citizens, bicameralism, term of office and recall, campaign money and lobbying, the franchise, constitution drafting (only Wikipedia mentions it), referendums and direct democracy, local government, minority and indigenous representation, and Gastil and Wright's Marxist postscript (Wright states there that the case for sortition fits progressive and conservative views alike, so its economics is not the ideology's). Advocates split on whether lots replace elections, so those answers are 0 at low confidence. Guerrero's original paper could not be opened (see notFound). Failing the uncertainty rule is the honest result.
